title: 3D Ising criticality with Platonic lattice superconducting qubits
authors: Liyang Sui, Hong-Hao Song, Sainan Huai, Yufan Li, Zhiwen Zong, Kunliang Bu, Xiaopei Yang, Xingrui Liu, Wenyan Jin, Bowen Chen, Xutao Zhang, Jianlan Wu, Yicong Zheng, Shengyu Zhang, Gang v. Chen, Yi Yin
abstract: The three-dimensional (3D) Ising model is a foundational model in statistical physics and critical phenomena, yet its analytical intractability has long impeded the precise determination of universal critical exponents. While high-precision estimates have been obtained through classical numerical methods and conformal bootstrap techniques, a direct quantum simulation of the 3D Ising criticality remains challenging, requiring nontrivial connectivity, sufficient system size, and high spectral resolution. In this work, assisted by the state-operator correspondence of conformal field theory, we perform a digital quantum simulation of the 3D Ising critical exponents using a multiply-connected 9-qubit superconducting quantum processor with a Platonic lattice geometry. Employing an extended variational quantum eigensolver equipped with a phase-based loss function, we variationally prepare the low-energy eigenstates of the transverse-field Ising model on a cubic Platonic lattice encoded in an 8-qubit register. The four lowest eigenenergies are extracted via Fourier-transform analysis and high-precision numerical fitting, agreeing with the exact diagonalization values up to +/- 0.001. The resulting scaling dimension Delta_epsilon = 1.5850 and critical exponent nu = 0.7067 match well with theory.
summary: The research demonstrates how to use superconducting qubits on Platonic lattices to digitally simulate the complex physics of 3D Ising criticality. By employing advanced VQE and time-evolution analysis techniques, the authors successfully extract key critical exponents that validate theoretical predictions. This establishes a powerful blueprint for using quantum computation to solve intractable problems in condensed matter statistical mechanics.
main_problem: The primary goal is to determine the universal critical exponents of the analytically intractable three-dimensional (3D) Ising model using quantum simulation techniques.
main_result:
The quantum simulation successfully extracted scaling dimensions ($\Delta_\epsilon = 1.5850$) and critical exponents ($
u = 0.7067$) that show strong agreement with established theoretical predictions from conformal field theory.
method: A hybrid quantum-classical approach combining an extended Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) protocol with time-evolution analysis via Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is used to extract low-lying energy eigenvalues.
model_or_system: The system models the 3D Ising criticality using the Transverse-Field Ising Model Hamiltonian ($H_p$) implemented on superconducting qubits arranged in Platonic lattice geometries (e.g., cubic lattice).
key_observables:
Critical exponents ($
u, \eta$), scaling dimensions ($\Delta_\sigma, \Delta_\epsilon$), and low-lying eigenenergies of the TFIM.
important_parameters: The critical transverse field ($h_c/J = 2.46$) and lattice connectivity (e.g., 12 edges for a cube).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that low-lying energy levels are sufficient to characterize the universal critical behavior, and it relies on mapping continuum CFT operators onto discrete qubit eigenstates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate state-operator correspondence between TFIM spectra and 3D Ising CFT spectra; time-domain signals show clear spectral peaks in Fourier transforms confirming extracted eigenenergies.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical link (state-operator correspondence) to detailing the quantum simulation protocol (VQE, phase-based loss function), demonstrating eigenvalue extraction via DFT on superconducting hardware, and finally calculating critical exponents using these measured spectral properties.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, near-term experimental pathway for probing fundamental concepts in statistical mechanics—namely, universal critical phenomena—using solid-state quantum hardware.
